knowledge_graph.title: Lafora disease
knowledge_graph.description: Lafora disease is a rare, autosomal recessive genetic disorder which results in myoclonus epilepsy and usually results in death several years after the onset of symptoms. The disease is characterized by the accumulation of inclusion bodies, known as Lafora bodies, within the cytoplasm of the cells.
knowledge_graph.causes: Mutation in either the EPM2A or EPM2B, genes
knowledge_graph.other_names: Lafora progressive myoclonic epilepsy, or MELF
knowledge_graph.prognosis: Universally fatal; most of the time, death occurs within 10 years after onset of initial symptoms
knowledge_graph.usual_onset: Late childhood and adolescence, usually ages 8–19 years

related_questions.snippet: What is the life expectancy of someone with Lafora disease? Most children diagnosed with Lafora disease survive up to 10 years after symptoms begin. Many live into early adulthood.

text_blocks.snippet: Lafora disease is caused by mutations in either the EPM2A gene or the NHLRC1 gene. These genes provide instructions for making proteins called laforin and malin, respectively. Laforin and malin play a crucial role in regulating glycogen metabolism and preventing the accumulation of abnormal glycogen deposits called Lafora bodies within nerve cells.
snippet_highlighted_words: mutations in either the EPM2A gene or the NHLRC1 gene

list.title: Genetic Basis:
list.snippet: Lafora disease is an inherited condition passed down through families in an autosomal recessive pattern. This means that a person must inherit a mutated copy of either the EPM2A or NHLRC1 gene from both parents to develop the disease.

list.title: Protein Function:
list.snippet: Laforin and malin work together to regulate glycogen, a stored form of glucose, within cells. Specifically, they help control the size and structure of glycogen molecules and prevent them from clumping together into insoluble Lafora bodies.

list.title: Lafora Bodies:
list.snippet: In Lafora disease, mutations in either EPM2A or NHLRC1 lead to a buildup of these abnormal glycogen deposits (Lafora bodies) in the brain and other tissues.

list.title: Neurological Damage:
list.snippet: These Lafora bodies disrupt normal cell function and cause progressive damage to nerve cells, leading to the characteristic symptoms of Lafora disease, including myoclonic epilepsy and cognitive decline.

related_questions.question: Can Lafora disease be cured?
related_questions.snippet: No curative treatments or preventative interventions are available at present for Lafora disease. Management of Lafora disease focuses on symptomatic relief of seizures and myoclonus, together with palliative, supportive, and rehabilitative measures.

related_questions.snippet: Seizures associated with Lafora epilepsy have mixed response to treatment, becoming less effective as the disease progresses. Affected dogs are typically euthanized by 10-12 years of age due to decline in quality of life.

text_blocks.snippet: Lafora disease is a rare, inherited, and fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by seizures, cognitive decline, and myoclonus (muscle jerks). It typically manifests in adolescence and leads to severe dementia and death within a few years. There is currently no cure, and management focuses on symptom relief and supportive care.
snippet_highlighted_words: a rare, inherited, and fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by seizures, cognitive decline, and myoclonus (muscle jerks)

list.title: Inherited:
list.snippet: It's caused by mutations in the EPM2A or NHLRC1 genes, which are involved in glycogen metabolism.

list.title: Neurodegenerative:
list.snippet: The disease causes progressive damage to the brain, leading to a decline in cognitive function and motor skills.

list.title: Seizures:
list.snippet: Both focal and generalized seizures, including myoclonic and tonic-clonic seizures, are common.

list.title: Myoclonus:
list.snippet: Sudden, involuntary muscle jerks, often triggered by movement or light, are a hallmark symptom.

list.title: Cognitive Decline:
list.snippet: Progressive loss of cognitive abilities, including memory, language, and executive functions, occurs.

list.title: Dementia:
list.snippet: Severe dementia develops in the later stages of the disease.

list.title: Poor Prognosis:
list.snippet: Lafora disease has a poor prognosis, with death typically occurring within 5-10 years of onset.

list.title: Seizures:
list.snippet: Focal (partial) seizures, including occipital seizures (vision loss and hallucinations), as well as generalized tonic-clonic seizures (stiffening and jerking).

list.title: Myoclonus:
list.snippet: Sudden, involuntary muscle jerks, often triggered by movement, light, or sound.

list.title: Cognitive Decline:
list.snippet: Memory loss, confusion, difficulty with speech and language, and impaired judgment.

list.title: Motor Impairment:
list.snippet: Ataxia (loss of coordination), spasticity (muscle stiffness), and loss of motor skills.

list.title: Behavioral Changes:
list.snippet: Emotional disturbances, depression, and changes in personality.
Clinical Examination: Doctors will assess symptoms, seizure patterns, and neurological function.
EEG: An electroencephalogram (EEG) can detect abnormal brain wave activity associated with seizures.
MRI: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can reveal brain abnormalities.
Skin Biopsy: A skin biopsy can show the presence of Lafora bodies (abnormal glycogen deposits) in the sweat ducts, which is a key diagnostic feature.
Genetic Testing: Molecular genetic testing can identify mutations in the EPM2A or NHLRC1 genes.
No Cure: Currently, there is no cure for Lafora disease.
Symptomatic Treatment: Management focuses on controlling seizures with anti-epileptic medications, managing myoclonus, and providing supportive care.
Palliative Care: As the disease progresses, palliative care becomes increasingly important to manage symptoms and improve quality of life.
Researchers are actively working on developing new treatments to target the underlying cause of the disease and potentially slow or stop its progression.

Research efforts focus on understanding the disease's mechanisms and developing therapies to degrade or prevent the formation of Lafora bodies, as well as treatments that can break down the accumulated glycogen.
